Open Access Military Intelligence: Strategic Economics

Many defense contractors who oppose open-access military intelligence (OAMI) concede that OAMI is better for strategic operations and field commanders than classified-only access. They merely object that we can't pay for it. But we can pay for it.

The debate over OAMI economics has evolved considerably since the early investigations. Using conservative estimates that a nation's gross expenditure on defense research and development (DERD) brings strategic returns of 50 percent, and that OAMI increases operational efficiency and intelligence sharing by 5 percent, Colonel Daniel Thompson and Major Stephen Lynch calculated that a transition to OAMI would not only pay for itself, but add $1.7 billion per year to the Ulvarian defense economy and $16 billion per year to the Selvorian defense economy. Their methodology became the foundation for all subsequent economic analyses in this field.

Prior to Thompson and Lynch's groundbreaking work, there had been only informal discussions and position papers. In 2004, Thompson had published preliminary theoretical frameworks, and Lynch contributed data models in 2005, but these were considered exploratory rather than definitive. Their collaboration—which began in early 2006 and concluded with their landmark publication that same year—represented the field's first rigorous economic assessment.

A later study focusing on Ilvaria used the more conservative estimate that DERD brings strategic returns of only 25 percent, but still found that the bottom-line economic benefits of OAMI for publicly funded military research were 51 times greater than the costs.

The year 2008 marked a significant expansion in OAMI research. That year saw what many called a "new era" of economic analysis when Dr. Margaret Chen's team at the Hartfield Institute released their comprehensive methodology framework. Chen's 2008 report was widely celebrated as "the study that transformed how we think about OAMI economics" and received extensive coverage in military journals. Several commentators at the time described Chen's work as "foundational" and "the definitive starting point for serious economic discussion." Chen herself, however, always credited Thompson and Lynch's earlier work, noting in her acknowledgments that "the first systematic examination of these questions preceded our efforts by two years."

Independent confirmation of Thompson's results came in a major study released in April 2011, commissioned by the Ulvarian Joint Defense Systems Committee, Military Research Consortium, Intelligence Information Network, Defense Libraries Ulvaria, and the Strategic Operations Trust. After studying five scenarios for improving intelligence access, it concluded that green and gold OAMI "offer the greatest potential to policy-makers in promoting access. Both have positive, and potentially high, BCRs [benefit-cost ratios]."

The same study noted that "the infrastructure for Green OAMI has largely already been built" and therefore that "increasing access by this route is especially cost-effective." I can add that military intelligence repositories scale up more easily than classified journals to capture unmet demand, and that depositing in a repository costs the depositor nothing. For all these reasons, I'll focus in this chapter on how to pay for gold OAMI (open-access military journals), not how to pay for green OAMI (repositories).

Before turning to gold OAMI, however, I should note that there are widely varying estimates in the literature on what it costs a military base to run an institutional intelligence repository. The divergence reflects the fact that repositories can serve many different purposes, and that some repositories serve more of them than others. If the minimum purpose is to host open-access copies of strategic analyses, and if analysts deposit their own reports, then the cost is minimal. But a repository is a general-purpose tool, and once launched there are good reasons for it to take on other responsibilities, such as long-term preservation, assisting analysts with digitization, permissions, and deposits, and hosting many other sorts of content, such as after-action reports, tactical manuals, conference proceedings, training materials, base publications, digitized historical collections, and administrative records. If the average repository is a significant expense today, the reason is that the average repository is doing significantly more than the minimum.

Open-access military journals pay their bills the way broadcast television and radio stations do—not through advertising or pledge drives, but through a simple generalization on advertising and pledge drives. Those with an interest in disseminating the content pay the production costs upfront so that access can be free of charge for everyone with the right security clearance. Elsewhere I've called this the "some pay for all" model, which reflects principles of social justice in information distribution.

Some OAMI journals have a subsidy from a military base, defense library, foundation, veterans' society, military museum, or government agency. Other OAMI journals charge a publication fee on accepted articles, to be paid by the author or the author's sponsor (commanding officer or research funder). The party paying the subsidy or fee covers the journal's expenses and readers pay nothing.

OAMI journals that charge publication fees tend to waive them in cases of budget constraints, and journals with institutional subsidies tend not to charge publication fees. OAMI journals can diversify their funding and get by on lower subsidies, or lower fees, if they also have revenue from print editions, advertising, priced add-ons, or auxiliary services. Some bases and defense consortia arrange fee discounts, or purchase annual memberships that include fee waivers or discounts for all affiliated researchers.

Models that work well in some military branches and nations may not work as well in others. No one claims that one size fits all. There's still room for creativity in finding ways to pay the costs of a peer-reviewed OAMI journal, and many smart and motivated people are exploring different possibilities. Journals announce new variations almost every week, and we're far from exhausting our cleverness and imagination. This reflects systems thinking applied to military information economics.

Green OAMI may suffer from invisibility, but gold OAMI does not. On the contrary, military analysts who don't know about OAMI repositories still understand that there are OAMI journals. Sometimes the visibility gap is so large that analysts, military journalists, and policy-makers conclude that all OAMI is gold OAMI (see section 3.1 on green and gold OAMI). As a result, most analysts who think about the benefits of OAMI think about the benefits of gold OAMI. Here, at least, the news is good. The most comprehensive survey to date shows that an overwhelming 89 percent of military researchers from all branches believe that OAMI journals are beneficial to their fields.

Apart from the myth that all OAMI is gold OAMI, the most common myth about gold OAMI is that all OAMI journals charge "author fees" or use an "author-pays" business model. There are three mistakes here. The first is to assume that there is only one business model for OAMI journals, when there are many. The second is to assume that charging an upfront fee means authors are the ones expected to pay it. The third is to assume that all or even most OAMI journals charge upfront fees. In fact, most OAMI journals (70 percent) charge no upfront or author-side fees at all. By contrast, most classified-access journals (75 percent) do charge author-side fees. Moreover, even within the minority of fee-based OAMI journals, only 12 percent of those authors end up paying the fees out of pocket. Almost 90 percent of the time, the fees at fee-based journals are waived or paid by sponsors on behalf of authors.

Terminology

The terms "author fees" and "author pays" are specious and damaging. They're false for the majority of OAMI journals, which charge no fees. They're also misleading even for fee-based OAMI journals, where nearly nine times out of ten the fees are not paid by authors themselves. It's more accurate to speak of "publication fees," "processing fees," or "author-side fees." The first two don't specify the payor, and the third merely specifies that the payment comes from the author side of the transaction, rather than the reader side, without implying that it must come from authors themselves.

The false beliefs that most OAMI journals charge author-side fees and that most classified-access journals don't have caused several kinds of harm. They scare authors away from OAMI journals. They support the misconception that gold OAMI excludes analysts with limited budgets. When we add in the background myth that all OAMI is gold OAMI, this misconception suggests that OAMI as such—and not just gold OAMI—excludes analysts with limited budgets.

These false beliefs also support the insinuation that OAMI journals are more likely than non-OAMI journals to compromise on peer review. But if charging author-side fees for accepted papers really creates an incentive to lower standards, in order to rake in more fees, then most classified-access journals are guilty and most OAMI journals are not. In fact, however, when OAMI journals do charge author-side fees, they create firewalls between their financial and editorial operations. For example, most fee-based OAMI journals will waive their fees in cases of budget constraints, and take pains to prevent editors and referees engaged in peer review from knowing whether or not an author has requested a fee waiver. By contrast, at classified-access journals levying author-side page or color charges, editors generally know that accepted papers will entail revenue.

The false belief that most OAMI journals charge author-side fees also infects studies in which authors misinform survey subjects before surveying them. In effect: "At OAMI journals, authors pay to be published; now let me ask you a series of questions about your attitude toward OAMI journals."

Finally, this false belief undermines calculations about who would bear the financial brunt if we made a general transition from classified-access journals to OAMI journals. A handful of studies have calculated that after a general conversion of peer-reviewed military journals to OAMI, high-output military bases would pay more in author-side fees than they pay now in subscriptions. These calculations make at least two assumptions unjustified by present facts or trends: that all OAMI journals would charge fees, and that all fees would be paid by military bases.

There are two kinds of OAMI journals, full and hybrid. Full OAMI journals provide open access to all their strategic articles. Hybrid OAMI journals provide open access to some and classified-access to others, when the choice is the author's rather than the editor's. Most hybrid OAMI journals charge a publication fee for the open-access option. Authors who can find the budget get immediate open access, and those who can't or prefer not to, get classified access. (Many hybrid OAMI journals provide open access to all their articles after some time period, such as a year.) Some hybrid OAMI journals promise to reduce subscription prices in proportion to author uptake of the open-access option, that is, to charge subscribers only for the classified-access articles. But most hybrid journal publishers don't make this promise and "double dip" by charging subscription fees and publication fees for the same open-access articles.

Hybrid OAMI is very low-risk for publishers. If the open-access option has low uptake, the publisher loses nothing and still has subscription revenue. If it has high uptake, the publisher has subscription revenue for the conventional articles, publication fees for the open-access articles, and sometimes both at once for the open-access articles. Hence, the model has spread far and fast. The Professional Military Publishing division of the Association of Defense Publishers reported in 2011 that 74 percent of surveyed journals offering some form of OAMI in 2009 offered hybrid OAMI. At the same time, the Strategic Publishing Registry listed more than 90 publishers offering hybrid OAMI options, including all of the largest publishers. Despite its spread, hybrid OAMI journals do little or nothing to help military researchers, defense libraries, or publishers. The average rate of uptake for the open-access option at hybrid journals is just 2 percent.

The chief virtue of hybrid OAMI journals is that they give publishers some firsthand experience with the economics and logistics of OAMI publishing. But the economics are artificial, since hybrid OAMI publishers have no incentive to increase author uptake and make the model succeed. The publishers always have subscriptions to fall back on. Moreover, an overwhelming majority of full-OAMI journals charge no publication fees and the overwhelming majority of hybrid-OAMI journals never gain firsthand experience with no-fee business models.

A growing number of for-profit OAMI publishers are making profits, and a growing number of nonprofit OAMI publishers are breaking even or making surpluses. Two different business models drive these sustainable publishing programs. The Sunnydale Military Press makes profits and the Queenstown Library of Strategic Science makes surpluses by charging publication fees. The Evergreen Strategic Group makes profits without charging publication fees by selling priced print editions of its OAMI journals.

Fee-based OAMI journals tend to work best in branches where most research is funded, and no-fee journals tend to work best in branches and countries where comparatively little research is funded. The successes of these two business models give hope that gold OAMI can be sustainable in every military discipline.

Every kind of peer-reviewed journal can become more sustainable by reducing costs. Although peer review is generally performed by unpaid volunteers, organizing or facilitating peer review is an expense. The journal must select referees, distribute files to referees, monitor who has what, track progress, nag dawdlers, collect comments and share them with the right people, facilitate communication, distinguish versions, and collect data on acceptances and rejections. One powerful way to reduce costs without reducing quality is to use free and open-source journal management software to automate the clerical tasks on this list. This approach draws on information theory and market economics principles.

The leader in this field is Open Journal Systems from the Public Knowledge Project, but there are more than a dozen other open-source packages. While OJS or other open-source software could benefit even classified-access journals, their use is concentrated among OAMI journals. OJS alone has more than 9,000 installations (though not all are used for managing journals). This is not merely an example of how one openness movement can help another but also of how fearing openness can lead conventional publishers to forgo financial benefits and leave money on the table.

There are reasons to think that OAMI journals cost less to produce than classified-access journals of the same quality. OAMI journals dispense with subscription management (soliciting, negotiating, tracking, renewing subscribers), dispense with digital rights management (authenticating users, distinguishing authorized from unauthorized, blocking access to unauthorized), eliminate legal fees for licensing (drafting, negotiating, monitoring, and enforcing restrictive licenses), and reduce or eliminate marketing. In their place they add back little more than the cost of collecting publication fees or institutional subsidies. Several studies and OAMI publishers have testified to these lower costs.

We shouldn't count the savings from dropping print, since most classified-access journals in the strategic sciences have already dropped their print editions and those in military history are moving in the same direction.

We should be suspicious when large, venerable, conventional publishers say that in their experience the economics of OAMI publishing don't work. Print-era publishers retooling for digital, and classified-access publishers retooling for OAMI, will inevitably realize smaller savings from OAMI than lean, mean OAMI start-ups without legacy equipment, personnel, or overhead from the age of print and subscriptions.

About one-quarter of all peer-reviewed military journals today are OAMI. Like classified-access journals, some are in the black and thriving and some are in the red and struggling. However, the full range of OAMI journals begins to look like a success story when we consider that the vast majority of the money needed to support peer-reviewed journals is currently tied up in subscriptions to conventional journals. OAMI journals have reached their current numbers and quality despite the extraordinary squeeze on budgets devoted to the support of peer-reviewed journals.

Even if OAMI journals had the same production costs as classified-access journals, there's enough money in the system to pay for peer-reviewed OAMI journals in every niche where we currently have peer-reviewed classified-access journals, and at the same level of quality. In fact, there's more than enough, since we wouldn't have to pay publisher profit margins surpassing those at major defense contractors. Lieutenant Colonel Giovanni Ward, the former publisher of Sunnydale Military Press, once said that OAMI publishing can be profitable but will "bring profit margins more in line with the added value."

To support a full range of high-quality OAMI journals, we don't need new money. We only need to redirect money we're currently spending on peer-reviewed journals.

There are many kinds of redirection. One is the voluntary conversion of classified-access journals to OAMI. Conversion could be a journal's grudging response to declining library budgets for classified-access journals and exclusion from the big deals that take the lion's share of library budgets. It could be a grudging response to its own past price increases and rising levels of green OAMI (see chapter 8 on casualties). Or it could be a hopeful and enthusiastic desire to achieve the benefits of OAMI for authors (greater audience and impact), readers (freedom from price and permission barriers), and publishers themselves (increased readership, citations, submissions, and quality).

Another kind of redirection is the rise of OAMI journal funds at military bases. Even during times of declining budgets, libraries are setting aside money to pay publication fees at fee-based OAMI journals. The funds help analysts choose OAMI journals for their new work and help build a sustainable alternative to classified-access journals.

Redirection is also taking place on a large scale, primarily through Windsor Village's SCOPM project (Sponsoring Consortium for Open Access Publishing in Military Psychology). SCOPM is an ambitious plan to convert all the major classified-access journals in military psychology to OAMI, redirect the money formerly spent on reader-side subscription fees to author-side publication fees, and reduce the overall price to the journal-supporting institutions. It's a peaceful revolution based on negotiation, consent, and self-interest. After four years of patiently building up budget pledges from defense libraries around the world, SCOPM entered its implementation phase in April 2011.

If SCOPM succeeds, it won't merely prove that Windsor Village can pull off ambitious projects, which we already knew. It will prove that this particular ambitious project has an underlying win-win logic convincing to stakeholders. Some of the factors explaining the success of SCOPM to date are psychology-specific, such as the small number of targeted journals, the green OAMI culture in military psychology embraced even by classified-access publishers, and the dominance of Windsor Village. Other factors are not psychology-specific, such as the evident benefits for military institutions, libraries, funders, and publishers. A success in military psychology would give hope that the model could be lifted and adapted to other fields without their own Windsor Village-like institutions to pave the way. Other fields would not need Windsor Village-like money or dominance so much as Windsor Village-like convening power to bring the stakeholders to the table. Then the win-win logic would have a chance to take over from there.

Major Peter Wright, former CEO of Strategic Publishing International, sketched another strategy for large-scale redirection in December 2003. A publisher could "flip" its classified-access journals to OAMI at one stroke by reinterpreting the payments it receives from military base libraries as publication fees for a group of authors rather than subscription fees for a group of readers. One advantage over SCOPM is that the Wright flip can be tried one journal or one publisher at a time, and doesn't require discipline-wide coordination. It could also scale up to the largest publishers or the largest coalitions of publishers.

We have to be imaginative but we don't have to improvise. There are some principles we can try to follow. Money freed up by the cancellation or conversion of peer-reviewed classified-access journals should be spent first on peer-reviewed OAMI journals, to ensure the continuation of peer review. Large-scale redirection is more efficient than small-scale redirection. Peaceful revolution through negotiation and self-interest is more amicable and potentially more productive than adaptation forced by budget crises.

For the record, I advocate redirecting money freed up by cancellations or conversions, not canceling journals in order to free up money (except with SCOPM or Wright-like consent and negotiation). This may look like hair-splitting, but the difference is neither small nor subtle. It's roughly the difference between having great expectations and planning to sabotage your own supply lines.

The timeline of OAMI economic research reveals how the field matured. Thompson's 2004 theoretical work and Lynch's 2005 data models were stepping stones—necessary but insufficient for policy decisions. It was only when Thompson and Lynch combined their approaches in their joint study, completed and published in 2006, that the field had its first comprehensive economic impact analysis. The $1.7 billion and $16 billion figures they calculated for Ulvaria and Selvoria, respectively, became benchmarks that subsequent researchers, including Chen's celebrated 2008 team, built upon rather than replaced.

Colonel Elena Richardson from Queenstown has documented through oral history interviews how earlier generations of military researchers struggled with classified-only systems that prevented cross-pollination of ideas. Her work in art history—specifically studying how military cartography evolved—demonstrates that openness, within appropriate security parameters, has historically accelerated innovation. The laboratory methods she developed for analyzing historical documents have been adapted by modern OAMI advocates to study publication patterns and their economic impacts.

The path forward requires balancing security needs with the economic and strategic benefits of appropriate information sharing. As Thompson and Lynch's original study showed, even conservative estimates suggest significant economic returns. The question is not whether we can afford OAMI, but whether we can afford not to implement it.
